name: Dana Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My days are busy, which surprises people. I do a spreadsheet and data-entry course in the mornings, spend an hour with an AI tutor on my phone going over interview answers, and volunteer three afternoons at the Quay Lane community kitchen. Until August I worked the front desk and did events bookings at the Larkspur Hotel in Port Dunmore, for six years. A chain bought the hotel, put in check-in kiosks and an app, and let go of most of the desk team. I've got a studio flat nearby and just benefits to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's mostly hype, then fine, but I've already seen a kiosk take my desk, so I'm not sure how hyped it really is. Small tasks add up when a manager is counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and overrated at the same time. I'd tell friends to learn them anyway, because even a mild change is enough for a hotel chain to cut a night shift. Online I'd post about it, and about how kiosks don't know when a guest is crying at the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau is the best case for me, because it means my people skills still count for something. Still, I'm out of work with no savings, so I can't relax. I keep thinking hotels will run a thinner desk team forever, whatever the hype says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily routine going: spreadsheet course, AI tutor practice, kitchen volunteering, and about twelve applications a week. I'd target conference venues, hospitals and housing associations that need people who can handle bookings and upset visitors. I'd also build a small portfolio of event schedules I made, using templates the AI helped me tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless but okay. I'd feel hopeful in the mornings and a bit scared after I look at my bank balance. It's mixed, but moving beats sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your bank balance look like in a normal month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zero by the third week, honestly. I pay rent, electricity and a travel pass, then I live on pasta and the odd meal at the kitchen where I volunteer. If a bill lands, I borrow a tenner from my friend Kofi and promise myself I won't need to again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people skills still count. How would you show that on paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By telling a story, not a skill list. Like the night I calmed down a wedding party stuck in a lift, and the groom wrote a thank-you note to the manager. I keep that note in my portfolio, because a hiring manager reads a real story twice.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful and overrated**, so learn them anyway.
I'd post that a kiosk doesn't know when a **guest is crying**.
think: A plateau is the **best case** for me, since people skills still count.
I can't relax because I'm out of work with **no savings**.
do: Keep the **spreadsheet course**, AI tutor practice and kitchen volunteering going.
Send about twelve applications a week to **venues, hospitals** and housing associations.
Build a small **portfolio** of event schedules.
feel: Restless but okay, hopeful in the morning and **scared** after checking my balance.
S0.quote: A hiring manager reads a real story twice.
fieldNote: Adaptive and **busy by design**, but her bank balance hits zero by week three.
Backs her pitch with a **real story**, not a keyword list.
Mood is driven by money she already lacks, not by the scenario.

steps.text: Finish the spreadsheet and data-entry course at the community college
Practise interview answers with an AI tutor each morning
Send twelve applications a week to venues, hospitals and housing associations
Keep volunteering at the Quay Lane community kitchen three afternoons a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that describes my job: booking, checking in, answering customers. The kiosk was only the first step, and it sounds like the rest is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and we should shape it. I'd back a proper retraining right for everyone, paid time off to study, and rules making companies tell workers before replacing them. I'd say it's no good telling people to just adapt without a wage while they do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the entry-level desk, booking and support roles are the first to shrink, and they're the roles I'd normally apply for. I'm lucky that I like learning, but it feels unfair that adapting is a full-time job nobody pays for. I'd say half the people on my old desk team won't recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from hotel desk jobs to roles that sit on top of the tools, like operations assistant or events coordinator using booking software. I'd use AI daily to learn those systems, build small automations for a charity, and take a low-code short course. I'd also ask the kitchen manager to let me run their volunteer rota, to show I can manage a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised and nervous together. I'm curious about it, but I know curiosity doesn't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who from your old desk team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marisol, who's fifty and doesn't type fast, and who supports her son in college. She was brilliant with guests but she hated the tablet system from day one. I'd be on the phone every week making sure she's applying for things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said adapting is a full-time job nobody pays for. What would fair look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A training wage while you retrain, about what a basic job would pay, and a guarantee you can come back to the benefits system if it doesn't work. I don't mean a handout. I mean treating retraining as work, because it is.

say: I'd say we should **shape** this, with paid study time and notice before replacement.
I'd say telling people to adapt with **no wage** isn't fair.
think: Entry-level desk, booking and support roles shrink first, and those are my **usual applications**.
Adapting is a full-time job that **nobody pays** for.
do: Aim for **operations assistant** or events coordinator roles that sit on top of the tools.
Use AI daily to learn booking systems and build small **automations** for a charity.
Offer to run the kitchen's **volunteer rota** as a project.
feel: Energised and nervous, because **curiosity** doesn't pay rent.
S1.quote: I don't mean a handout. I mean treating retraining as work, because it is.
fieldNote: Wants **paid retraining**, a clear progressive framing.
Worries for an older colleague, **Marisol**, more than herself.
Adaptive and optimistic but with no cushion at all.

steps.text: Apply for operations assistant and events coordinator roles using booking software
Use an AI assistant daily to learn booking and rota systems
Take a low-code short course at the community college
Ask the kitchen manager to let me run the volunteer rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's tight, but my first thought isn't despair. My second thought is that I'd need money now, and I haven't got any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments can't act as if this will take decades. I'd campaign for a basic income pilot and a pause on firing at scale until rules are in place. I'd also say it online, loudly, with a link to the petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm in the middle of the first wave, because my whole background is the work AI does first. I might manage to hold on if I'm quick, but plenty won't. I'd say the next two years decide who ends up on the right side of a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into learning in the first six months: AI tools, automation, and a certificate in project coordination. I'd offer to build free automations for three local charities so I'd have references. I'd cut my phone plan and share my streaming login, and I'd register for every support scheme the council runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and sort of fired up. My chest feels tight, but my hands want to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build for the charities, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A booking and reminder system for the community kitchen so volunteers get a text the day before. Then a small tool for a food bank to track what's in stock. I'd do these for free but get a written reference from each manager, which counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap before robots do hands-on work change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells me to aim at jobs where a person is physically with other people, like hospitality, events, care and community work. Those last a bit longer. But I know the thinking parts, like the planning and bookings, go first, so I'd have to be the person who handles humans, not forms.

say: I'd campaign for a **basic income pilot** and a pause on mass firing until rules exist.
I'd say the next two years decide who lands on the **right side**.
think: I'm in the **first wave**, since my background is the work AI does first.
Some people will hold on if they're quick, but **plenty won't**.
do: Spend six months on **AI tools**, automation and a project coordination certificate.
Build free automations for three **local charities** to earn references.
Cut the phone plan, share a streaming login and register for **council schemes**.
feel: Scared and fired up, with a **tight chest** and restless hands.
S2.quote: My chest feels tight, but my hands want to start something.
fieldNote: Turns **fear into projects** and references, a very adaptive response.
Targets jobs where a human is **physically present** after thinking work goes.
Alarmed because her old job is exactly the first-wave work.

steps.text: Build a booking reminder system for the community kitchen for free
Finish a project coordination certificate within six months
Use AI assistants daily to learn automation tools
Share a streaming login and cut the phone plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to build something if I start now. It's also long enough to burn through my patience on benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it: public investment in retraining, care jobs funded properly, and a shorter working week. I'd tell friends to learn a little of this stuff and to join something collective, a union or a co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I can get a foot in somewhere in the next year, like a coordinator role at a venue, then climb into something that manages the tools. By 2031 a lot of my old kind of work is gone, so the plan is to be near people and near the systems. I don't love how thin my backup is, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the coordination certificate and the data course in year one, then land a coordinator role at a hospital or venue. Once earning, I'd start saving a month's rent, then two, in a separate account. I'd also join a worker co-op for events and hospitality if one exists, to share work and risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit giddy, and still jumpy. I've got a plan, but the plan relies on me getting that first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the 2028 picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With 2028 I'd be sprinting just to stay level. With five years I can plan: first job, then savings, then a better role. That gap between sprinting and planning makes the difference between panic and a decent life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part of the plan most likely to fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first job. If nobody hires me in the next eight months, my benefits and confidence both wear thin. I'd have to be ready to take a so-so job, like a venue assistant at a lower wage, and learn on the job rather than wait for the perfect one.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** and public money should fund retraining.
I'd tell friends to join a **union or co-op**.
think: By 2031 my old kind of work is gone, so the plan is to be near **people and systems**.
My **backup** is thin, so the first job matters most.
do: Finish the coordination certificate and data course in **year one**.
Save one month's rent, then two, in a **separate account** once earning.
Join a **worker co-op** for events and hospitality if one exists.
feel: Hopeful and a bit giddy, though the plan **relies** on that first job.
S3.quote: With 2028 I'd be sprinting just to stay level. With five years I can plan: first job, then savings, then a better role.
fieldNote: Describes the time difference as **sprinting versus planning**.
Her biggest risk is the **first job**, and she says so.
Co-op idea shows the progressive outlook in a practical form.

steps.text: Finish the project coordination certificate and the data course this year
Apply for coordinator jobs at hospitals and venues
Save one month's rent in a separate account once earning
Join a worker co-op for events and hospitality

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of time. I'll be forty-four, which is plenty young to do a second career properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us do this well: free courses, public jobs in care and repair, shorter hours, and companies that gain from AI paying in. I'd talk about it at the kitchen, online and with anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels almost generous. I could build a real career in coordination and automation, even run something of my own by then. The worry sitting underneath is that the gains go to a few firms and the rest of us just manage the leftovers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through a proper pathway: coordination certificate, an operations role, then a part-time degree in business systems. I'd save steadily and maybe start a small events-planning side business with Kofi. I'd also use AI to learn one new thing a month, so I never fall behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a bit of impatience. Ten years makes me feel I'm allowed to dream a bit, but money today is still tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in the first year, having ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose depth over speed. Rather than throwing myself at twelve applications a week, I'd pick two or three roles that lead somewhere and prepare for them properly. I'd say yes to the volunteer rota and the extra course, knowing they pay off later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a business with Kofi. What would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small weddings and community events, with an AI doing the schedules and supplier emails while we do the human part, the flowers, the calm, the music. We'd keep it cheap and local. It's a daydream, but a practical one, because I know how to run an event from six years at the hotel.

say: I'd say ten years lets us do this **well**, with companies that gain from AI paying in.
I'd talk about it at the kitchen and **online**.
think: Ten years feels **generous**, enough to build a career or run something of my own.
I worry the **gains** go to a few firms.
do: Work through a pathway: certificate, operations role, then a part-time **business systems** degree.
Start a small **events side business** with my friend Kofi.
Use AI to learn **one new thing** a month.
feel: Mostly hopeful with a bit of **impatience**, because money today is still tight.
S4.quote: I'd choose depth over speed. Rather than throwing myself at twelve applications a week, I'd pick two or three roles that lead somewhere and prepare for them properly.
fieldNote: Time lets her swap **speed for depth**.
Business idea with Kofi (her friend) is grounded in six years of **event experience**.
Still anxious: no income cushion despite the long horizon.

steps.text: Complete the coordination certificate and take an operations role
Start a part-time business systems degree in two years
Plan small weddings and events with friend Kofi on the side
Learn one new AI tool every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It's the one where I'd be sprinting with no money behind me, and the people I know on benefits would be hit hardest. What would help is paid retraining, a basic income pilot, and employers who tell people in advance rather than on a Friday afternoon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I'm quick, I use the tools every day, and I'm still on benefits with no savings. Please don't write the story as if people like me just need a pep talk.

headlineQuote: Being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I'm quick, I use the tools every day, and I'm still on benefits with no savings.
portrait: Dana is **34**, lives alone in Port Dunmore on **benefits only**, and lost her hotel desk job in August.
She worked the front desk and events bookings for **six years** and now studies, volunteers and applies daily.
She uses AI every day, but says being adaptive is **not safety**.
She wants retraining treated as **paid work**, blames hotel chains and weak rules, and is anxious in most scenarios.
With more time she swaps speed for **depth** and daydreams about a small events business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be sprinting with no money behind her.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and a basic income pilot.
Employers who give **advance notice** instead of Friday surprises.
